## Proof

We work in the Banach space $L_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with the usual norm $\|f\|_1 = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |f|\,dm$. Recall that
$$X = \bigl\{ f \in L_1(\mathbb{R}^n) : m\bigl(f^{-1}((0,\infty))\bigr) = 0 \bigr\} = \{ f \in L_1 : f \le 0 \text{ a.e.}\}.$$

We claim that **$X$ is closed but not open**.

---

### $X$ is closed

Let $(f_k) \subset X$ with $f_k \to f$ in $L_1$. We must show $f \in X$, i.e. $f \le 0$ a.e.

A standard consequence of $L_1$-convergence (via the Borel–Cantelli argument / Riesz–Fischer) is that there exists a subsequence $(f_{k_j})$ converging to $f$ **pointwise almost everywhere**. Let $E$ be the null set off which $f_{k_j}(x) \to f(x)$, and let $N_j$ be the null set off which $f_{k_j} \le 0$ (these exist since $f_{k_j} \in X$). Set
$$N = E \cup \bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty} N_j, \qquad m(N) = 0.$$
For every $x \notin N$ we have $f_{k_j}(x) \le 0$ for all $j$ and $f_{k_j}(x) \to f(x)$, so by pointwise convergence of a sequence of non-positive numbers,
$$f(x) = \lim_{j\to\infty} f_{k_j}(x) \le 0.$$
Thus $f \le 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus N$, i.e. $f \le 0$ a.e., hence $m(f^{-1}((0,\infty))) = 0$ and $f \in X$. Therefore $X$ contains all its $L_1$-limit points and is **closed**.

---

### $X$ is not open

Consider $f \equiv 0$, which clearly belongs to $X$ (since $f^{-1}((0,\infty)) = \emptyset$). We show $f$ is **not** an interior point of $X$.

For any $\varepsilon > 0$, let $B = B(0,r)$ be a ball with $0 < m(B) < \infty$ (e.g. the unit ball) and set
$$g = \varepsilon \cdot \mathbf{1}_B.$$
Then $g \in L_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and
$$\|g - f\|_1 = \|g\|_1 = \varepsilon \cdot m(B),$$
which can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $\varepsilon$ small. Yet $g > 0$ on $B$, and $m(B) > 0$, so $m(g^{-1}((0,\infty))) = m(B) > 0$, meaning $g \notin X$.

Hence every $L_1$-neighborhood of $f \equiv 0$ contains a point outside $X$, so $0$ is not an interior point of $X$. Therefore $X$ has empty interior (in particular $X^\circ = \emptyset$) and $X$ is **not open**.

---

### Conclusion

The set $X = \{f \in L_1(\mathbb{R}^n) : m(f^{-1}((0,\infty))) = 0\}$ is **closed** in $L_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ but **not open**. Equivalently, $X$ is a proper closed cone (the non-positive cone) with empty interior.

### PROOF COMPLETE
